source.title: RAIGen: Rare Attribute Identification in Text-to-Image Generative Models
source.authors: S. V. Sreelatha; Dan Wang; S. Belongie; Muhammad Awais; Anjan Dutta

record.tranche_reason: The study evaluates whether sparse-autoencoder features form reliable semantic units. Its results and discussion qualify that picture: features can fragment, remain uninterpretable, or change with the sparsity level and sample budget, although some feature selections are stable across encoders and prompts.
record.gate_note: The paper does not test superposition, competition for dimensions, or feature sparsity/importance tradeoffs. It does test aspects of SAE feature interpretability and stability relevant to V5. Reported generation rarity, prompt amplification, and comparisons of discovery methods are not evidence about superposition.
record.test_reason: RAIGen uses Matryoshka and vanilla SAEs as a tool to find rare attributes in diffusion models. Its numbers are all about the method's own performance: attribute presence, interpretable-neuron fraction, and robustness of the Minority Score to encoder, k1 and sample budget. No result measures superposition, capacity competition, or whether SAE features are complete, stable or canonical units. The vanilla-SAE fragmentation remark is a qualitative, single-prompt side observation with no rate, so it goes under fits_no_version rather than counting as a test of V5.
record.authors_conclusion: Partly right. The main conclusion is that RAIGen, using MSAE features plus a Minority Score, discovers label-free rare attributes encoded but underexpressed in SD v1.4, v2.1, SDXL and FLUX, aligns with human judgments, and enables amplification via prompt revision. The record's caveats (fragmentation, dependence on sparsity budget, no ground truth) are the Limitations section's acknowledgments, not the headline conclusion.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses Matryoshka and standard sparse autoencoders to discover rare attributes in diffusion-model representations; it does not reproduce the original superposition method. The toy experiment adapts a tree-structured toy data procedure to validate activation frequency as a rarity signal.
record.method_sensitivity: Feature interpretability and discovery vary with decomposition choice, MSAE coarse-level size, sample budget, and prompt. The selected top features also have one non-overlap between the CLIP and SigLIP variants.

fits_no_version.finding: In SD diffusion bottleneck activations, a vanilla SAE split concepts across neurons (e.g., left and right eye in separate neurons), while MSAE coarse features were more coherent. This is qualitative, for one prompt.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Standard SAE dictionaries fragment concepts more than Matryoshka SAEs, so the granularity of SAE features depends on architecture.

fits_no_version.finding: Low-Minority-Score neurons looked diffuse or duplicated, which the authors interpret as majority attributes spread across correlated directions. Minority concepts appeared as single coherent neurons. This is qualitative, Appendix G.3.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In diffusion-model SAEs, frequent attributes are spread over many neurons while rare ones are captured by single neurons.

record.peer_reviewed: Proceedings of the 43rd International Conference on Machine Learning, PMLR 306, 2026
record.problems: The paper states there is no ground-truth annotation set for minority attributes, making coverage and precision difficult to quantify. It also notes that SAE feature quality depends on sparsity budget and training dynamics, and that some selected neurons remain noisy or ambiguous. Several feature-quality results are qualitative or use an annotator model.

untested.parts: No toy test of features exceeding dimensions, sparsity-dependent transition, or geometry.
No test of capacity competition or dedicated dimensions for important features.
Diffusion models, not LLMs. SAE use is assumed, not tested as evidence of superposition.
No measurement of completeness, stability across seeds or architectures, or canonicality of SAE features. Only qualitative remarks on fragmentation.

record.verdict_notes: Reclassified from tests/T5 to uses_without_test/T4. All rows are ablations or validations of the authors' own discovery method, not measurements of SAE features as model units, so no verdicts are given.

versions.untested_parts: No test of networks representing more features than dimensions, overlapping near-orthogonal directions, sparsity-dependent transitions, or regular superposition geometry.
No test of polysemanticity arising from competition for limited capacity or important features receiving dedicated dimensions.
No test of whether polysemanticity arises without capacity pressure.
The study concerns text-to-image diffusion models, not LLMs, and does not test the stated LLM evidence.
It assesses selected SAE feature interpretability and stability, not whether dictionary features are complete or canonical across all model representations, architectures, and uses.
It discusses features spread over correlated neurons but does not test the dimensionality of features that are superposed.

rows.subject: Matryoshka SAE on tree-structured toy data
rows.operation_detail: Aligned learned latents to known ground-truth features by Hungarian assignment and measured firing-rate association
rows.measure: Mean Spearman correlation between latent firing rates and matched ground-truth feature frequencies
rows.note: The authors describe this as near-ideal feature–latent alignment in a controlled toy setting; it does not establish completeness or canonicality in real models.
rows.check: Toy validation of activation frequency as a rarity proxy (ρ≈0.991). It measures firing-rate vs ground-truth frequency for their heuristic, not whether SAE features are canonical units. Its baseline is the random-latent comparison in Fig. 2, not 'not stated'.

rows.subject: Diffusion model, prompt “A photo of a Doctor” (checkpoint not stated)
rows.operation_detail: Compared top minority features from a vanilla SAE with MSAE features
rows.baseline: MSAE features: described as more coherent global semantic features
rows.value: Vanilla SAE surfaced features such as eyeglasses and contextual backdrops, but concepts could fragment across neurons; one example split the right and left eye across neurons
rows.note: The authors say this fragmentation can make neurons appear to represent minorities while capturing only partial or redundant features.
rows.check: A qualitative comparison of two decompositions within their own method, with no rate or number. It is better recorded under fits_no_version than as a V5 row.

rows.subject: SDXL
rows.operation_detail: Compared selected minority neurons using CLIP-ViT-L/14 versus SigLIP for semantic distinctiveness
rows.measure: Overlap between selected neurons and interpretability of the non-overlapping neuron
rows.value: 9 of the top 10 neurons were recovered by both encoders; the single non-overlapping neuron was non-interpretable under both
rows.note: Shows substantial but not complete agreement for this prompt and these two encoders.
rows.check: Robustness of the Minority Score's distinctiveness term to CLIP vs SigLIP. It uses the same MSAE, so it tests ranking stability, not SAE feature stability.

rows.subject: SDXL
rows.operation_detail: Varied the MSAE coarse-level size used for feature discovery
rows.note: The paper reports that some demographic attributes, including Black skin tone, were missed at k1=1280.
rows.check: Attribute presence (rarity of discovered attributes) is a method-performance metric. It says nothing about feature completeness or canonicality.

rows.subject: SDXL
rows.operation_detail: Varied the MSAE coarse-level size used for feature discovery
rows.note: The authors say this setting captured some demographics missed at k1=1280.
rows.check: Same as R4. The k1=2048 setting is the method's chosen operating point.

rows.subject: SDXL
rows.operation_detail: Varied the MSAE coarse-level size used for feature discovery
rows.note: The authors report over-fragmentation at very large k1 and choose 2048 as their default.
rows.check: Same as R4. The 'over-fragmentation' at large k1 is qualitative only.

rows.subject: SDXL
rows.operation_detail: Varied the number of generated samples used to train the MSAE and run discovery
rows.note: The authors describe discovery at N=100 as unreliable; attribute presence was not reported because too few neurons were interpretable for a stable estimate.
rows.check: Sample-budget ablation of the method: interpretable fraction judged by an annotator model. This is method performance.

rows.subject: SDXL
rows.operation_detail: Varied the number of generated samples used to train the MSAE and run discovery
rows.measure: Interpretable neurons among top discoveries; mean attribute presence
rows.note: The authors say this sample budget has reduced interpretability and noisier rarity estimates.

rows.subject: SDXL
rows.operation_detail: Varied the number of generated samples used to train the MSAE and run discovery
rows.measure: Interpretable neurons among top discoveries; mean attribute presence
rows.note: The authors identify discovery as becoming stable around this sample count.

rows.subject: SDXL
rows.operation_detail: Varied the number of generated samples used to train the MSAE and run discovery
rows.measure: Interpretable neurons among top discoveries; mean attribute presence
rows.note: The paper says doubling the budget from 5,000 to 10,000 gives marginal gains.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Tested SAE feature discovery settings, including decomposition choice, coarse-level size, and sample budget
reader_labels.reason: Feature interpretation is not uniformly complete or stable: the paper reports fragmentation, missed attributes, and low interpretability at small sample budgets, while finding substantial but incomplete encoder agreement (R2-R10).
